title: Sacking A Piece in the Alapin | The Sensei Speedrun | Grandmaster Naroditsky

moves.spoken: We take White and meet the Sicilian — today we play normal theory, then deliberately sacrifice a piece and show how to fight back from a lost position.
We open the Alapin with c3.
The c-pawns come off on d4.
We develop the knight to c3 — though the bishop to g5 would have been a fine chance to hang it; now Black just plays ...Nf6.
Black pins with the bishop to b4 — and here's our chance: we play the bishop to g5.
We play the bishop to g5 — a believable blunder, and at least it develops a piece. The comedy would be if Black declined it.
Black develops the knight to f6.
We even offer the bishop to a6 — all but begging Black to win material; it's oddly hard to give a piece away.
Black takes on c3 with check.

Black wins our bishop, the pawn recapturing on a6 — the sacrifice is complete, and we've even traded off another pair of minors, making it harder on ourselves. Now the recovery begins, a full piece down. First, know this: ...e5 does not win the knight back — after ...h6, the bishop to h4, ...g5 unpins, and if the bishop drops to g3 the knight is free. Basic, but essential.
So we play e5 — in a situation like this it's a genuine attempt to complicate the game.

Black plays h6. It slightly weakens his structure, but down a piece a small weakness isn't enough — we need something concrete. The idea is to take on f6: after ...hxg5 we push to g7, and even after ...Rg8 we defend the g7-pawn indirectly with the queen to h5 — if the rook grabs g7, the queen forks on h8. Recovery rarely comes in a single move: build tension and sow doubt.
Black wins our bishop, recapturing on g5.

We push to g7 and set the queen toward h5, sowing doubt. This game is really about recovery technique when you're lost, and the principles are these. Complicate — pose your opponent decision after decision, because decisions breed fatigue and doubt. Keep your pieces active — bring the rook in with h4 rather than a timid g3, and ask the "Shankland question": what happens if you just do it anyway, developing and ignoring a pawn? Defend key pawns by developing, not by a passive king move — a rook to d3 both guards c3 and prepares to lift to g3. Manoeuvre the knight toward a dream square like d6, via f7. Use a break like d5 not only to lure the bishop off b7 but to open lines and strip away defenders. And once you win material back, convert with a passed pawn — push it hard while the opponent is passive, escort it with a rook cutting off the king, and finish with the ladder-mate technique, bringing your own king up to guard the checking square so the rooks can deliver mate. Even dead lost, purposeful, problem-posing play saves a remarkable number of games.
